y1-calculus: Both develop calculus and mathematical problem-solving. UCR extends to differential-equation modelling and Mathematica; Radboud additionally includes probability.
y1-mathstruct: Both develop sets, relations, propositional and predicate logic, induction and mathematical proof. Radboud also specifies number theory; UCR adds formal game and process modelling.
y1-matrix: Both develop linear systems, matrix operations, vector spaces, linear maps and eigenvalues. UCR extends to orthogonality, least squares and singular-value decomposition.
core-algorithms: Both study data structures, asymptotic efficiency, algorithm design and graph algorithms. UCR also introduces computability, reductions and complexity classes.
core-complexity: Both analyse asymptotic algorithmic complexity. UCR develops algebraic algorithms and optimisation; Radboud additionally gives a dedicated treatment of complexity classes and NP-completeness.
y1-imperative: Both develop structured programming, control flow, functions, recursion and data structures. UCR uses Python and includes object orientation; Radboud uses Rust and adds its own algorithms and complexity sequence.
y1-database: Both study relational databases, their theoretical basis and SQL implementation. Radboud additionally develops conceptual information modelling; UCR’s description does not establish an identical modelling project.
core-functional: Both teach functional programming with Haskell, including functions, recursion and types. UCR divides its course between Haskell and object-oriented C++ development, testing and software quality; it is not the full dedicated Radboud sequence.
core-os: Both study processes, threads, concurrency, synchronisation and memory management. UCR combines operating systems with network protocols and experimental investigations; Radboud additionally requires separate network-security study.
y1-ai: Both address reasoning under uncertainty in intelligent systems. UCR develops probabilistic models and decision theory; Radboud also surveys search, machine learning and social aspects.
y1-analysis: Both use R to explore and visualise data. UCR develops data cleaning, transformation and text/spatial workflows; Radboud additionally specifies introductory statistical inference.
core-reflection: Both develop academic skills, study reflection and personal direction. UCR also includes academic writing and civic engagement; Radboud maintains a computing-specific portfolio and mentorship sequence.
core-methods: Both develop research questions, design, ethical inquiry and reliable evidence. UCR includes empirical data collection and statistical analysis; Radboud gives specific attention to computing research, user studies and stakeholders.
core-society: Both critically examine how computing technologies affect society and institutions. UCR focuses on AI’s business, economic, labour and governance consequences; Radboud also develops philosophical questions about privacy, politics and knowledge.
